topics.label: Plate Tectonics
facts: Earth's outer layer is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates that move very slowly.
The plates float on hot, soft rock deep inside Earth.
Where plates push together, mountains can form, and where they pull apart, new crust can form.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen at the edges where plates meet.

choices: Huge pieces of Earth's outer layer that move very slowly
questions.fact: Earth's crust and upper mantle are broken into plates that drift a few centimetres a year.

choices: Hot, soft rock deep inside Earth
questions.fact: Below the plates is the mantle, hot rock that can flow very slowly.

questions.q: What can form where two plates push together?
questions.fact: When plates collide, the crust crumples upwards and forms mountain ranges like the Himalayas.

questions.q: Where do most earthquakes and volcanoes happen?
questions.fact: Plate boundaries are where most of Earth's earthquakes and volcanoes occur.

topics.label: Types of Volcanoes
facts: Volcanoes erupt when magma rises from below Earth's crust and escapes at the surface.
Shield volcanoes have gentle slopes and runny lava, while stratovolcanoes are steep and can erupt explosively.
Volcanic ash can block sunlight and cool the climate for months after a huge eruption.
New islands, like those in Hawaii, are built by volcanoes erupting under the sea.

choices: Magma rises and escapes at the surface
questions.fact: Pressure builds as magma rises, and when it finds a crack it erupts.

questions.q: Which volcano has gentle slopes and runny lava?
questions.fact: Shield volcanoes, like those in Hawaii, are built by runny lava flowing long distances.

questions.q: What can volcanic ash do after a huge eruption?
choices: Block sunlight and cool the climate
questions.fact: Ash high in the sky reflects sunlight, cooling Earth for months.

questions.q: How were the Hawaiian islands built?
choices: By volcanoes erupting under the sea
questions.fact: Lava from underwater volcanoes piled up over millions of years to form the islands.

topics.label: How Earthquakes Work
facts: Earthquakes happen when stress builds up along a fault and the rocks suddenly slip.
The point inside Earth where an earthquake starts is called the focus, and the point on the surface above it is the epicentre.
Seismic waves are the vibrations that travel through Earth during an earthquake.
The Richter scale and the moment magnitude scale measure how much energy an earthquake releases.

choices: Rocks suddenly slipping along a fault
questions.fact: Stress builds up in rocks until they suddenly slip, releasing energy as seismic waves.

questions.q: What is the point on Earth's surface directly above where an earthquake starts?
questions.fact: The focus is where the quake starts underground; the epicentre is the point above it on the surface.

choices: Vibrations that travel through Earth during an earthquake
questions.fact: Seismic waves carry the energy of an earthquake through the ground.

questions.q: What do the Richter and moment magnitude scales measure?
choices: How much energy an earthquake releases
questions.fact: Magnitude scales measure the energy released by an earthquake.

topics.label: Mountains
facts: Mountains are tall landforms that rise high above the land around them.
Many mountains form where tectonic plates push together and the crust is forced upwards.
Mount Everest is the highest mountain on Earth, about 8,849 metres above sea level.
Mountain climates are colder at the top, and snow can stay on high peaks all year.

choices: Tectonic plates push together and force the crust upwards
questions.fact: Colliding plates crumple the crust upwards into mountain ranges.

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain on Earth?
questions.fact: Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level, at about 8,849 metres.

questions.q: Why is it colder at the top of a mountain?
choices: The air is thinner and holds less heat
questions.fact: Higher up, the air is thinner and cannot hold as much heat.

questions.q: What can stay on high mountain peaks all year?
questions.fact: On high peaks it stays cold enough for snow to last all year.
